result.markdown:
# Registering on PROSPERO and risk of bias {#sec-prospero}



Chapter 2 left us with a review we believe is viable: enough studies, enough
dose levels, a reference in each, and enough printed per level to reconstruct
the covariance. We also left it with a search strategy and an extraction
template. What we do not yet have is a public record of what we intend to do
with them.

This chapter is about writing that record. It is not a tour of the PROSPERO
form, because most of the form is the same form every systematic review fills
in, and there are better places to learn it than a book about one design. What
we do here is narrower and more useful: we go to the numbered questions where a
dose-response review says something a standard review never has to say, and we
write them. The record has twelve sections, and the ones that change are 1.5
Review objectives, most of Section 2 on eligibility, 7.2 to 7.4 on bias and
certainty, 8.1 Main outcomes, and, above all, 9.1 Strategy for data synthesis.
Each section below is named for the question as PROSPERO words it on screen,
and opens by giving the question's number and the size of box it expects, so
the chapter can be read with the form open.

One departure from the form's own order is worth announcing. We take 9.1 before
Section 7, because the synthesis plan is what gives the risk of bias ratings a
job, and it is hard to say what a rating is for before knowing what the model
will do with it.

The second half of the chapter rates the studies. Risk of bias sits in the same
class as registration because the rating scheme is declared in the protocol, and
a scheme chosen after the studies are in hand is a scheme chosen to get an
answer.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The two worked examples**

We carry forward the two data sets from Chapter 2, and we write a protocol for
each of them.

`aripiprazole` holds five randomized, double-blind, fixed-dose trials of
aripiprazole in schizophrenia, with the change in the Positive and Negative
Syndrome Scale reported as a mean and a standard deviation per dose arm. It is
the data behind Crippa and Orsini [-@crippa2016].

`alcohol_cvd` holds six exposure contrasts from four studies of alcohol intake
and cardiovascular disease, reported as an effect with confidence limits plus
the cases and totals per category. Four of those contrasts come from
case-control studies and two from studies reporting cumulative incidence.

Both come with the package, so `library(easyDR)` is all that is needed to
follow along. This chapter fits nothing, though, so no code is shown in it.
:::

## Why register, and when

Prospective registration on PROSPERO means lodging the protocol with the Centre
for Reviews and Dissemination at York before the review has produced any
results, and accepting that the record is public and versioned from then on.
Anybody can read what we said we would do, and compare it with what we did.

The timing rule is more generous than it sounds, and it is worth stating
plainly. **We register before data extraction begins.** Searching may be done.
Screening may be done. Deciding which studies meet the inclusion and exclusion
criteria may be done. What may not be done is extracting the numbers, because
the numbers are what the analysis plan is about, and a plan written after seeing
them is not a plan.

Why insist on this harder in a dose-response review than in an ordinary one?
Because this design has more defensible analyses than any other in the
meta-analytic family. Let us count them on the data we already have.
**{easyDR}** offers six functional forms, and all six are respectable choices
with literature behind them.


::: {#tbl-shapes-count .cell tbl-cap='The modelling choices a dose-response protocol has to commit to, with the defensible options in each.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Choice                       |Options                                                |
|:----------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|
|Functional form              |linear, log, quadratic, cubic, rcs, fp                 |
|Knot placement, for a spline |three knots, placed at any of five common percentiles  |
|Pooling stage                |two-stage or one-stage                                 |
|Reference level              |study reference, or re-expressed to a common one       |
|Dose assigned to a category  |midpoint, median, or a stated rule for open categories |


:::
:::


We see that five decisions are open before a single number is read, and that
none of them has one right answer. Multiply the options together and the same
extraction sheet supports well over a hundred analyses, each of which would
survive peer review on its own. Some of them will show a rising curve, some a
plateau, some a U shape. Choosing among
them after seeing all of them is the practice known as **researcher degrees of
freedom**, and in this design the freedom is unusually wide.

This is why `easydr()` has no default shape. Asking for a fit without naming
`shape` produces an error rather than a straight line, and the error lists what
may be written instead. The package refuses the choice because the choice is a
claim about biology, and the place for it is the protocol, with a reason beside
it.

::: {.callout-important}
**Registration is not the same as being first**

PROSPERO records are often treated as a claim on a topic. They are not. The
record protects the reader from us, by making our intentions checkable. A
registration that says "we will fit the most appropriate dose-response model"
protects nobody, even though it was lodged first.
:::

## Writing in the future, without setting it in stone

A protocol is written in the future tense. We will search, we will screen, we
will extract, we will fit. This is not a stylistic convention. The tense is the
evidence of when the document was written, and a protocol in the past tense is a
report wearing a protocol's clothes.

That leaves a genuine tension, and it is the one authors get wrong most often. A
protocol has to commit, or it offers no protection. Yet we cannot honestly
commit to a shape we have not seen data for, or to a departure-from-linearity
test whose result we do not know. Write it too tightly and we will break our own
protocol in month four. Write it too loosely and we have registered nothing.

The way out is to commit to the **rule** rather than to the **result**. A
conditional plan names three things: the trigger, the action that follows it,
and what gets reported either way. All three have to be in the sentence, because
a trigger with no stated action is a hint, and an action with nothing reported
when the trigger fails is a hidden choice.

Let us see the difference on one decision, the functional form.

> *We will fit the most appropriate dose-response model.*

That is a blank cheque. "Appropriate" is decided later, by us, using information
we do not have yet, and no reader can tell whether we kept the promise, because
the promise cannot be broken.

> *We will fit a restricted cubic spline with three knots at the 10th, 50th and
> 90th percentiles of the pooled dose distribution. If the test of departure
> from linearity gives $p$ < 0.05, the spline will be the primary model. If it
> gives $p$ ≥ 0.05, the linear model will be the primary model and the spline
> will be reported as a sensitivity analysis. Both curves will be shown in the
> supplement in either case.*

That is a plan. The trigger is a named test with a named threshold, the action
follows from it mechanically, and the reader gets both curves whichever way the
test falls, so there is nothing to be gained by hoping for one result.

::: {.callout-important}
**The test of a contingency**

Hand your protocol and your extraction sheet to a stranger. If that person
would arrive at the same primary model you did, you wrote a plan. If the person
would have to ask you what you meant, you wrote a preference.
:::

## The fields that differ from a standard review

Now to the form itself. The PROSPERO record has twelve sections and roughly
forty numbered questions, and most of them are filled in exactly as they would
be for any review. Let us go only to the ones this design forces us to word
differently, and let us call each by the number and the name it carries on
screen, so that the chapter can be read with the form open beside it.


::: {#tbl-fields .cell tbl-cap='The numbered PROSPERO questions a dose-response review answers differently, and what changes in each.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Question                                     |Changes                                                                                 |
|:--------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|1.5 Review objectives                        |Asks how the effect moves across the dose range, not whether an effect exists           |
|2.1 Population                               |Unchanged, with one addition: the dose range the population is exposed to               |
|2.2 Intervention(s) or exposure(s)           |Names the dose metric, its unit, and the rule for assigning a dose to a category        |
|2.3 Comparator(s) or control(s)              |A level rather than a group: each study's own reference, and whether it is re-expressed |
|2.4 Study design                             |Names the designs, and each design added here costs a tool in 7.2                       |
|7.2 Study risk of bias or quality assessment |One tool per design, named individually, never a bare 'JBI tools'                       |
|8.1 Main outcomes                            |One outcome per curve, with the effect measure stated beside it                         |
|9.1 Strategy for data synthesis              |The functional form, the knots, the pooling stage, the covariance method                |


:::
:::


We see that the changes are not scattered through the form. They cluster in
Section 2, which defines eligibility, and in Section 9, which defines the
analysis. Searching and screening, Section 6, changed too, but we settled that
in Chapter 2 when we agreed to keep the outcome out of the search string, and
it goes into 6.2 and 6.6 as written there.

Six questions deserve more than a table row.

### Review objectives

**Question 1.5**, 10 to 200 words, required.

A standard meta-analysis asks whether an exposure is associated with an outcome.
Our question is different in kind. We ask how the association **behaves** as the
dose rises: whether it climbs in a straight line, flattens after some intake,
reverses, or shows no trend at all. A protocol whose question is "is alcohol
associated with cardiovascular disease" has registered the wrong review, and
every field downstream will inherit the error.

Written out for our two examples:

> *To characterize the shape of the dose-response relationship between daily
> aripiprazole dose and change in the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale in
> adults with schizophrenia, and to estimate the dose producing 80 per cent of
> the maximum predicted response.*

> *To characterize the shape of the dose-response relationship between habitual
> alcohol intake, in grams of ethanol per day, and the risk of cardiovascular
> disease in general adult populations.*

Both say shape. Neither asks a yes-or-no question. PROSPERO allows 10 to 200
words here and asks that the objective be answerable with data that exists in
the included studies, which is the viability question of Chapter 2 arriving in
the form.

### Population

**Question 2.1**, an inclusion box and an exclusion box, 200 words each.

This question changes least, and it changes once. PROSPERO asks for inclusion
and exclusion criteria for the participants, as any review would. What a
dose-response review adds is the **range of exposure the population spans**,
because a population none of whose members reach a high dose cannot inform the
upper half of the curve, however many of them there are.

A cohort of lifelong light drinkers is a legitimate study of alcohol. It is
not a study that can tell us what happens at 60 grams a day, and a protocol
that says so in 2.1 will not be surprised later by a confidence band that opens
out at the right-hand edge of the figure.

### Intervention(s) or exposure(s)

**Question 2.2**, two boxes plus PICO tags.

This is the question with no counterpart in a standard review, and it is where
most of the later pain is prevented. PROSPERO gives two boxes, inclusion and
exclusion, up to 200 words each, plus PICO tags. Three things go in them.

The **unit** the dose is measured in, stated once and converted to at
extraction rather than later. The **rule for assigning one number to a
category**, because published papers report bands rather than doses. And the
range of doses the review will accept, which is the exclusion box.

The middle one is the part authors forget. A cohort reports intake as "1 to 14
grams per day", "15 to 29", and "30 or more". The first two have midpoints. The
third is open-ended and has none, so the protocol has to say in advance what we
will do with it. A common and defensible rule is to add the width of the
adjacent closed category to the open category's lower bound, which gives 45
grams per day here. Any rule will do, as long as it is written down before we
see which rule makes the curve look better.

> *Exposure will be expressed as grams of ethanol per day. Where a study reports
> intake in drinks or in another unit, we will convert using the ethanol content
> stated by that study, or 12 grams per standard drink where none is stated.
> Each exposure category will be assigned the dose reported by the authors where
> one is given, the midpoint of the category otherwise, and, for an open-ended
> highest category, its lower bound plus the width of the adjacent category. The
> reference category will be the lowest reported intake in each study.*

### Comparator(s) or control(s)

**Question 2.3**, three radio buttons and two boxes.

PROSPERO offers three radio buttons here and asks for the alternatives the main
intervention will be compared against. In an ordinary review the comparator is
a **group**. In ours it is a **level**, and each study supplies its own: placebo
or never-exposed where such a level exists, and the lowest reported category
otherwise.

That makes this question the right place for one decision Chapter 4 will act
on. Studies disagree about what the reference should be, and the estimates can
be re-expressed against a common reference before pooling [@hamling2008].
Whether we intend to do that is stated here, because a reader who sees "the
lowest reported category in each study" and then meets a common reference in
the results has caught us changing the comparator after the fact.

### Study design

**Question 2.4**, 250 words of inclusion and 150 of exclusion.

PROSPERO asks for the types of study eligible for inclusion, and the field
guide gives one instruction that saves trouble later: never write
"observational studies" as a design. Name them. Parallel randomised trial,
cluster randomised trial, prospective cohort, retrospective cohort,
case-control, cross-sectional, single-arm.

The reason to be exact is that **every design named here costs a tool in 7.2**,
and a dose-response review mixes designs more readily than other reviews do. A
single case-control study among nine cohorts adds a second risk of bias tool, a
second set of judgements to report, and a second covariance approximation in
the model. That may well be worth it. It should be a decision, not a
by-product.

::: {.callout-important}
**The three-level rule is a pooling rule, not an eligibility criterion**

It is tempting to write Chapter 2's viability steps into 2.4, so that a study
reporting two exposure levels is simply ineligible. Do not. A criterion written
into Section 2 removes the study from the review and from the table of
findings, and a two-level study still carries a highest-against-lowest
comparison we can use.

The rule belongs in **9.1 Strategy for data synthesis**, where it decides which
analysis a study enters rather than whether it exists. The same holds for the
requirement that a study report counts, or means with standard deviations: that
is a statement about what the model needs, and the model lives in 9.1.
:::

### Main outcomes

**Question 8.1**, and 8.2 takes the rest.

One curve belongs to one outcome. A review with three outcomes is three
dose-response analyses, and the primary one is named now, before we discover
which of the three has the most interesting shape.

PROSPERO asks for the outcome definition, the acceptable measurement
instruments, the timepoints, and **the effect measure to be used in synthesis**.
That last item is easy to skip and it is the one that has to agree with 9.1. A
dose-response review reports a trend per unit of dose, or an effect at a named
dose, so the effect measure written here is a risk ratio per gram per day, or a
mean difference at 20 mg per day, rather than a bare "risk ratio".

## Strategy for data synthesis, as a set of contingencies

**Question 9.1**, the only question of Section 9, 500 words.

Here is the box that carries the chapter, and the hardest one in the form. It
takes 500 words, and PROSPERO's own guidance is blunt about what fails: generic
text. A box reading "a random effects meta-analysis will be performed and
heterogeneity assessed with $I^2$" describes no review in particular, and a
record carrying it gets flagged as a template.

The field asks for ten things: what is pooled with what and the rule that
decides when studies are too different to pool; the effect measure per outcome,
matching 8.1; the model, its between-study variance estimator and its
confidence interval method; how heterogeneity will be quantified and what will
be done about it; the subgroups, with the hypothesis behind each; the
sensitivity analyses; what happens to studies that cannot enter a model;
missing data; unit of analysis issues; and the software with its version.

Let us write them as a sequence of conditional commitments, in the order the
analysis will meet them, each one naming its trigger and its action.

**The pooling stage.** Two-stage estimation fits a trend inside each study and
then pools the trends [@orsini2012]. It is the default in **{easyDR}** and the
usual primary choice, and it needs every study to carry at least three levels.
One-stage estimation fits every study inside a single mixed model [@crippa2019],
keeps studies that two-stage drops, and leaves no per-study estimate to draw.
The plan therefore reads as follows. Two-stage is primary where at least three
studies report three or more exposure levels with the information the
covariance needs. If fewer than three studies clear that bar, or if more than a
quarter of included studies report only two levels, one-stage becomes primary,
and the reason is reported.

**What is pooled with what.** One curve pools studies of the same exposure, in
the same population, against the same outcome, and the rule that decides when
studies are too different to pool is clinical rather than statistical. Two
exposures reported by the same cohort, beer and wine for instance, enter as
separate contrasts and the shared participants are declared as a limitation.

**The within-study covariance.** Estimates within a study share a reference
group, so they are correlated, and the correlation has to be reconstructed by
the method of Greenland and Longnecker [-@greenland1992], with the approximation
chosen by each study's design [@orsini2006]. The contingencies here are about
missing inputs. If a study reports effects and confidence limits but not the
counts behind them, it cannot enter the two-stage model, and we have already
said so in the eligibility criteria. For a continuous outcome the gap is usually
the reference group's standard deviation. Crippa and Orsini [-@crippa2016] name
the remedy: approximate it with the pooled standard deviation of the
non-reference levels. The protocol then adds the contingency, which is to vary
the imputed value in a sensitivity analysis and report whether the curve moved.

**The functional form.** We met the wording for this above. What the protocol
adds is the reason for the primary shape, and the reason comes from the exposure
rather than from the data: whether a plateau or a threshold is biologically
plausible, which dose range the readers care about, and what comparable reviews
fitted. For aripiprazole a plateau is expected, because a drug has a maximum
effect, so a spline is the primary model and a straight line would be the
surprise. For alcohol and cardiovascular disease the published literature is
split between a monotonic rise and a J shape, so both are named, with the spline
primary and the linear fit reported beside it.

**The knots.** Number and placement, in advance. Three knots at the 10th, 50th
and 90th percentiles of the pooled dose distribution is a defensible default and
the one Crippa and Orsini used. It is defensible, not sacred, and the honest way
to treat it is to declare the default and the sensitivity analysis in the same
breath: alternative placements drawn from combinations of the 10th, 25th, 50th,
75th and 90th percentiles, reported as a panel of curves. The contingency that
matters is what happens when they disagree. If the shape we report depends on
which placement we chose, the conclusion is that the shape is not established,
and the protocol commits us to saying so rather than to picking the panel we
like.

**What gets reported, and at which doses.** A fit with more than one term has no
single slope, so there is no one number to quote, and the protocol says the
result will be reported as a named shape together with effects at specific
doses. Those doses are declared now, through `at`, and they are chosen because
readers recognize them, not because the curve is interesting there. Every
estimate is reported against the reference dose, which `easydr()` prints with
each fit for exactly this reason.

**Dose findings.** If the pooled curve attains a maximum inside the observed
exposure range, we will report the dose at that maximum and the dose producing
80 per cent of the maximum predicted response, with confidence intervals from
the parametric bootstrap [@crippa2016]. The condition is doing real work. A
maximum at the edge of the observed range is an artefact of where the data
stopped, and a protocol that promises an optimal dose unconditionally will
produce one whether or not there is one.

**Heterogeneity.** Random effects by restricted maximum likelihood, with
Cochran's $Q$ reported. The sentence worth adding is that heterogeneity here
lives in the coefficients of a curve rather than in a single effect, so a lone
$I^2$ describes the pooled trend and not the agreement between shapes. The
study-specific curves will be plotted so the reader can see the disagreement
directly.

**Small-study effects.** Egger's regression if at least ten studies enter the
model, and if fewer, the funnel plot is inspected and no test is claimed. Below
ten studies the test has very little power, and a null result from eight studies
means almost nothing. **{easyDR}** prints that warning above the panel rather
than trusting us to remember it.

**Robustness.** A leave-one-out analysis, refitting the model with each study
omitted in turn, and a commitment to name in the results any study whose
omission moves the pooled trend materially or collapses the heterogeneity. A
pooled curve that rests on one cohort is a finding, not an inconvenience.

**Subgroups.** By study design, because design decides how each study's
covariance is approximated, and a set that mixes case-control with cumulative
incidence is carrying two approximations at once. No test of the difference
between levels is planned. Two subgroups estimated from four studies and from
two will differ by some amount whatever the truth is, so the protocol commits us
to comparing intervals and stating how few studies each one rests on.

**Studies that cannot enter the model.** This is where Chapter 2's viability
steps belong, and where we promised in 2.4 to put them. A study reporting two
exposure levels, or reporting effects without the counts behind them, cannot
carry a trend. It is not dropped from the review. It enters the
highest-against-lowest comparison, it appears in the table of findings, and the
protocol says in which analyses it is counted and in which it is not.

**Missing data.** What will be requested from authors, what will be imputed and
what will be excluded. The gap specific to this design is the reference group's
standard deviation in a continuous review, handled as above. A gap in the
counts cannot be imputed, so it moves the study to the comparison rather than
the curve.

**Unit of analysis.** A dose-response study is a multi-arm study by
construction, and every one of its arms is measured against one reference.
Counting those arms as independent studies is the error this whole design
exists to avoid, so the protocol states that each study contributes one trend,
or one set of curve coefficients, however many exposure categories it reported.

**Software.** Named with its version, because a spline basis and a knot
placement are implementation details as much as statistical ones. For this book
that is _R_, with **{easyDR}** calling **{dosresmeta}** [@dosresmeta].

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Reporting it: the data synthesis field**

The continuous example, as it would be lodged:

> *Study-specific dose-response curves will be estimated by generalized least
> squares, accounting for the covariance between mean differences sharing a
> common placebo arm, and the resulting coefficients will be pooled by
> multivariate random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum likelihood.
> The primary model will be a restricted cubic spline with three knots at the
> 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of the pooled dose distribution. Results will
> be reported as the predicted change in score at 5, 10, 15, 20 and 30 mg per
> day relative to placebo and, if the pooled curve attains a maximum within the
> observed dose range, as the dose at that maximum and the dose producing 80 per
> cent of the maximum predicted response, with bootstrap confidence intervals.
> Sensitivity analyses will vary knot placement, substitute a fractional
> polynomial and a quadratic model, and omit each trial in turn.*

The binary example differs in four places, and they are the four that always
differ:

> *Within-study covariances will be reconstructed by the method of Greenland and
> Longnecker, using the approximation appropriate to each study's design.
> Studies will be pooled by two-stage random-effects meta-analysis, with
> one-stage estimation reported as a sensitivity analysis. The primary model will
> be a restricted cubic spline with three knots at the 10th, 50th and 90th
> percentiles of the pooled intake distribution, with the linear model reported
> beside it and the test of departure from linearity used to decide which of the
> two is primary. Risk ratios will be reported at 10, 20 and 30 grams of ethanol
> per day against the study reference level. Subgroup analyses by study design
> are planned; no formal test of subgroup difference will be performed.*
:::

::: {.callout-important}
**Extrapolation is a protocol commitment**

The most common over-reach in this literature is reading a curve beyond the
doses the studies actually observed. That is not a discussion-section problem to
be handled tactfully later. It belongs in the analysis plan, as a sentence
saying that effects will be reported only within the observed exposure range and
that the range will be marked on every figure.
:::

## Study risk of bias or quality assessment

**Question 7.2**, a radio, then tool checkboxes and a method radio.

There is no risk-of-bias tool for dose-response meta-analysis, and we should be
glad of it. The thing being rated is a study, and what a study needs rated
depends on how it was conducted, not on what we intend to do with it afterwards.
So we choose the tool by design, exactly as the course does.

PROSPERO makes this a click. The question is "Will risk of bias be assessed?",
and a yes opens a list of tools to tick: Cochrane RoB-1, Cochrane RoB-2, JBI
tools, Newcastle-Ottawa, PROBAST, QUADAS-2, QUADAS-C, ROBINS-E, ROBINS-I,
ROBIS, Other. The designs we named in 2.4 decide which ones are ticked.


::: {#tbl-rob .cell tbl-cap='The risk of bias tool follows the design of the study being rated, named as PROSPERO lists it.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Design                                  |Tool                                    |
|:---------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|
|Randomised trial                        |Cochrane RoB-2                          |
|Non-randomised study of an intervention |ROBINS-I                                |
|Cohort study of an exposure             |ROBINS-E                                |
|Case-control study                      |JBI, Checklist for Case Control Studies |
|Single-arm study or case series         |JBI, Checklist for Case Series          |


:::
:::


Two details of this screen are worth knowing before it is reached. **JBI tools
opens into individual checklists**, and ticking the parent without naming the
checklist leaves the record ambiguous, so the table above names each one. And
**one tool per design, no more**: a record listing five tools for a review of
eight trials reads as a copied checklist, and the obvious question at peer
review is which tool was used on which study.

Dose-response reviews mix designs more often than other reviews do, because the
exposure is a quantity and quantities get measured in whatever study happens to
record them. A review may hold randomized fixed-dose trials and observational
cohorts at once. The protocol then names more than one tool and says which study
gets which, and it says one thing more: ratings from different tools are not
comparable, so they will be reported per tool rather than counted into a single
tally of low-risk studies.

Our two examples land on different tools, and for the binary one the reason is
printed in the data. Let us look at it.


::: {#tbl-designs .cell tbl-cap='The design of each study in the binary example, as the extraction sheet recorded it.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Study             |Design               |
|:-----------------|:--------------------|
|Bianchi           |case-control         |
|Bobak             |case-control         |
|Malarcher-wine    |case-control         |
|Malarcher-beer    |case-control         |
|Vliegenthart-wine |cumulative incidence |
|Vliegenthart-beer |cumulative incidence |


:::
:::


We see that four of the six contrasts come from case-control studies and two
from studies reporting cumulative incidence, which means one review needs two
tools. The cumulative incidence studies are observational studies of an
exposure, so they are rated with **ROBINS-E**, and the case-control studies are
rated with the **JBI Checklist for Case Control Studies**. The five
aripiprazole studies, by contrast, are randomised, double-blind, fixed-dose
trials, so a single tool serves for all of them, and it is **Cochrane RoB-2**.

PROSPERO also asks how the rating will be done, and the answer is the ordinary
one: independently by two reviewers, disagreements resolved by discussion and
by a third reviewer where needed, with authors contacted for clarification.

### The domain that matters most here

Among the domains any of these tools asks about, one carries more weight in a
dose-response review than it would anywhere else: **exposure measurement**.

The reason is worth a paragraph, because it is not obvious. In a review of a
single high-against-low contrast, error in measuring the exposure blurs the
contrast and widens the interval. In a dose-response review it does something
worse. Non-differential error in the dose does not scatter the curve evenly: it
pulls high doses down and low doses up, which flattens the trend toward the
null. A review built on studies that measured intake with a single
food-frequency questionnaire will therefore tend to find a shallower curve than
the truth, and a shallow curve is easy to read as reassuring. The protocol says
in advance that exposure measurement will be rated for every study and reported
alongside the pooled slope.

Confounding deserves one sentence of the same kind, for observational reviews.
Studies differ in what they adjusted for, and the protocol says which estimate
we will extract when a paper reports several. The maximally adjusted estimate is
the usual answer, and it is only usable if we say so before we see which
adjustment set gives the steeper curve.

### Reporting bias assessment

**Question 7.3**, a radio and a 50 word box.

The next question asks whether risk of bias due to missing results will be
assessed, and the answer is yes, in a box of fifty words. What goes in it is
already decided, because we committed to it in 9.1: contour-enhanced funnel
plots, and Egger's test when at least ten studies contribute to a
meta-analysis.

The ten-study threshold is the part to keep. Below it the funnel plot and the
asymmetry test say almost nothing, and promising one anyway is a small fiction
that has to be explained later. Alongside it, trial registry entries and
protocols are compared with the publications, which catches the outcome a paper
measured and did not report.

### Certainty assessment

**Question 7.4**, a radio and 5 to 250 words, required.

The last question of Section 7 asks whether certainty of findings will be
assessed, and a yes commits us to GRADE across risk of bias, inconsistency,
indirectness, imprecision and publication bias, with randomised evidence
starting at high certainty and non-randomised at low.

This is where the ratings stop being decoration. A table in a supplement that
no later section refers to has no job; the GRADE assessment gives it one, and
so does the second use, which belongs in 9.1: a sensitivity analysis restricted
to studies not rated at high risk, declared in advance, including what we will
conclude if the restricted curve differs in shape from the full one.

Two commitments come with the yes, and both are easy to tick past. Saying yes
means producing a summary of findings table, which is the first thing a methods
reviewer looks for. And imprecision is judged against a decision threshold set
before the analysis, not against statistical significance. In a dose-response
review that threshold is a dose and an effect together: the smallest change in
risk, at a dose people are actually exposed to, that would alter advice.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Reporting it: the risk of bias field**

> *Randomised trials will be assessed with Cochrane RoB-2. Cohort studies of
> exposure will be assessed with ROBINS-E, and case-control studies with the
> JBI Checklist for Case Control Studies. Two reviewers will rate each study
> independently, with disagreements resolved by discussion and by a third
> reviewer where needed. Ratings will be reported by tool and will
> not be combined across tools. A sensitivity analysis will refit the primary
> model excluding studies rated at high risk of bias overall or at high risk in
> the exposure measurement domain. Certainty of evidence will be assessed with
> GRADE for the primary outcome.*
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Test your knowledge!**

1. A team has completed its search, screened titles and abstracts, and agreed a
   final list of 14 included studies. They have not opened a spreadsheet. Is it
   too late to register on PROSPERO, and why?
2. A protocol states: "We will test for non-linearity and report the better
   fitting model." Name the two things missing that would turn this into a plan.
3. A cohort reports alcohol intake as 0, 1 to 14, 15 to 29, and 30 or more
   grams per day. Which numbered PROSPERO question has to settle this before
   the study can be extracted, and why does it have to be written first?
4. A team writes "studies must report at least three exposure categories" into
   2.4 Study design. Why is that the wrong field, where does the requirement
   belong, and what does the study lose if it stays in 2.4?
5. A review includes four randomised dose-finding trials and seven cohorts. How
   many tools does 7.2 name, and what does the record say about combining their
   ratings?

Answers to these questions are listed in Appendix A.
:::

## Summary

- Prospective registration happens before data extraction begins. Searching and
  screening may already be complete, because the analysis plan is about numbers
  we have not yet read.

- A dose-response review has more defensible analyses than any other
  meta-analytic design, since the functional form, the knots, the pooling stage,
  the reference level and the dose assigned to each category are all genuine
  choices. The protocol is what stops those choices from being made by the
  result.

- A protocol is written in the future tense, and it commits to rules rather than
  to results. A usable contingency names a trigger, the action that follows, and
  what will be reported whichever way the trigger falls.

- The questions that change are 1.5 Review objectives, which asks about shape
  rather than existence; 2.2 Intervention(s) or exposure(s), which names a
  metric, a unit and a rule for open-ended categories; 2.3 Comparator(s), where
  the comparator is a level rather than a group; 2.4 Study design, where each
  design named costs a tool in 7.2; 8.1 Main outcomes, which carries the effect
  measure; and 9.1 Strategy for data synthesis, which carries everything else.

- A requirement about what a study must report in order to enter a model is a
  pooling rule, not an eligibility criterion. It belongs in 9.1, not in Section
  2. Written into Section 2 it removes the study from the review and from the
  table of findings, when the study still carries a highest-against-lowest
  comparison we can use.

- The risk of bias tool follows the design of the study being rated: Cochrane
  RoB-2 for randomised trials, ROBINS-I for non-randomised intervention
  studies, ROBINS-E for cohort studies of an exposure, and the matching JBI
  checklist, named individually, for case-control studies and case series.

- Mixing designs means mixing tools. Ratings from different tools are reported
  separately rather than counted into one tally.

- Exposure measurement is the domain that matters most here, because error in
  the dose flattens the curve toward the null rather than widening it evenly.
